AbilityView.description:
One activated ability this card could be asked to activate right now
(`engine_api.list_abilities`, `serialize._card_view`'s `abilities`
key) - its own index (what `ActivateRequest.ability_index` names), plus
everything `affordances.ability_hints` reports about what activating it
would ask for.
AbilityView.title: AbilityView

Action.description:
The arguments one engine entry point takes - a serializable call spec.

Built so "what a seat took" and "what else was legal at that moment" are
the same type, directly comparable, and replayable from a log row long
after the `Game` that produced it is gone. Every reference to something in
the game is an id (`card_id`, `decision_candidates`, `attacker_id`) rather
than a live object - see the module docstring for why that is load-bearing
rather than a style preference.
Action.title: Action

ActionKind.description:
What kind of call spec this is - one entry point per engine action a
seat (or `legal_actions`) can name.
ActionKind.title: ActionKind

ActionOutcome.description:
The response shape of every action-mutating route
(`app._respond`/`app.audit_outcome`) - `engine_api.Outcome.body()` plus
the audit log's own `log_seq`.

`allowed` is `None` exactly when the action paused on an unanswered
decision (`paused=True`, `pending_decision` set) rather than completing
or being refused outright. Fields beyond the five declared here are
action-specific (`Outcome.detail` - e.g. `cost`, `tapped`, `spell_id`,
`ability_id`, `card_id`, `attackers`, `mana_ability`, `ability`) and are
deliberately **not** enumerated as named fields: `engine_api.Outcome
.detail` is untyped by design - each of its call sites across
`engine_api.py` builds a different key set for a different action, and
naming them all here would either claim a field a given route's response
never actually carries, or force one implausibly wide union. This model
instead declares the fields every mutating route's response shares and
lets the rest through as additional, unnamed properties
(`extra="allow"`) - the same honesty `serialize.state_view`'s own
dynamically-keyed fields get, extended to this genuinely per-action
shape. A consumer that needs one action's exact detail keys should pin
against that route's own example response, not against this component.

`notices` is the one `Outcome.detail` key declared here rather than left
to `extra="allow"`: unlike `cost`/`tapped`/`spell_id`/..., it is not
per-action - `commands.run_command` files it onto every command kind's
outcome generically (`commands._attach_notices`), so every route this
model serves can carry one. Each entry is one of `Game`'s 19 fail-closed
notice records (`{"kind": ..., **notice.model_dump(mode="json")}`, plus
this api's own `zone`/`controller` bookkeeping - see
`commands._new_notices`), already redacted for this response's own
viewer (`app.audit_outcome`) - not the engine's raw list.
ActionOutcome.title: ActionOutcome

ActionRow.description:
The engine's own `Action` as `GET .../legal-actions` serves it, plus
what the api adds to a row (`action_rows.legal_action_rows`). Every field
here is left off a row it does not apply to.
ActionRow.title: ActionRow

ActionTargets.description:
What one action may legally name, per requirement slot.

`understood: false` carries NO slots and a `note` saying why, which is
`affordances.candidates`' existing contract kept intact: an empty
candidate list would read as "nothing on this board is legal", a
different and false statement, and `ui/app.js`'s `isPickingTargets`
already branches on exactly that difference.
ActionTargets.title: ActionTargets

ActionWithTargets.description:
The engine's own `Action`, plus the candidates the api enumerates for
it (`app._attach_target_candidates`). A subclass rather than a re-shape:
every field of `Action` is passed through untouched and by inheritance,
so a field the engine adds arrives here without this file changing.

`targets` is **required**, which is what makes this a distinguishable
branch of `LegalActionsResponse.actions` rather than a replacement for
`Action` - see there.
ActionWithTargets.title: ActionWithTargets

ActorRequest.description:
An optional body for endpoints that take no other input: just who is
calling, so the audit log can attribute the action.
ActorRequest.title: ActorRequest

AdditionalCostHintView.description:
One optional additional cost this card may be cast with (CR 601.2b,
CR 118.8b) - `affordances.cast_hints`' own reading of the engine's
`machines/casting.optional_additional_costs`, the same enumeration
`Action.additional_cost_options` carries on a row.

On the card view rather than only on a row because this is what the
browser holds the moment the player picks the card up, before any
legal-actions row or affordance has been fetched - and a choice that is
not on screen before the cast is committed is a choice the player never
had.
AdditionalCostHintView.title: AdditionalCostHintView

AdditionalCostOption.description:
One optional additional cost this `CAST` action's spell may be cast
with (CR 601.2b, CR 118.8b) - Sowing Mycospawn's `Kicker {1}{C}`,
Everflowing Chalice's `Multikicker {2}`, Gigadrowse's `Replicate {U}`.

CR 601.2b: "If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will
be paid as it's being cast such as buyback or kicker costs ..., the
player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs".
CR 118.8b: "Some additional costs are optional."

Like `SpliceOption`, and unlike `spell_face`/`alternative_cost`, this is
not a family of mutually exclusive `Action`s: CR 118.8a lets any number
of additional costs apply to one cast, so the row carries the whole
space a seat may announce from and the announcement itself is made on
the cast (`Game.cast(kicker=..., offspring=..., ...)`).

It is deliberately *not* folded into `Action.cost`. CR 118.8d: "Additional
costs don't change a spell's mana cost, only what its controller has to
pay to cast it" - and nobody has announced this one yet, so adding it to
the displayed cost would claim a choice that has not been made, exactly
the reason an unannounced `{X}` is left alone there too.
AdditionalCostOption.title: AdditionalCostOption

AdvanceRequest.description:
Who is advancing the turn - required, unlike `ActorRequest`, because
`Game.advance` now authorizes the call against the active player (or
their controller, CR 723.5) rather than merely logging who asked.
AdvanceRequest.title: AdvanceRequest

AdvanceResponse.description:
`POST .../advance`'s paused-or-completed response - always the full
state view. The one branch with none at all (the engine's own refusal,
caught before `_run_command` ever attempted anything) is bare
`ActionOutcome` instead, so the route's real response type is
`ActionOutcome | AdvanceResponse`.
AdvanceResponse.title: AdvanceResponse

AdviceApproveIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/advice/{seq}/approve` - the human saying
yes to one proposal, by its ledger `seq`.

Human uid only. An advisor's own uid is refused by `game_access.py`
before this route ever runs (the path is neither `/advice` nor `/report`
and the body claims no `dry_run`), and the route checks the same thing
again against `store.player_for_uid`: an advisor must never be able to
approve its own advice, and that must hold whether or not the gate is
the thing enforcing it on any given day.
AdviceApproveIn.title: AdviceApproveIn

AdviceIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/advice` - one action an **advisor** thinks
its human should take, recorded and never performed.

An advisor credential (`repository.Advisor`) is read-only by
construction: `game_access.py` refuses every mutating POST it makes
except this one and `/report`. So this is not a convenience - it is the
only way a buddy pod reaches the game it is watching at all, and the
reason it is a *ledger row* rather than anything held in memory is that
the api is multi-replica: a proposal kept in one process would be
invisible to the replica the human's next poll happens to hit.

`method`/`path`/`body` are the **request the human's client will post
verbatim** once it agrees, built by `seatkit` (which already knows how to
shape every action) rather than hand-written by a model - see
`seatkit.Seat._advise_answer`. `body` names the human as `player` and
carries no `dry_run`: an approved proposal is a real action.

There is deliberately no `summary` field here. What the proposal *says*
is derived server-side from `body` and the live game
(`records.advice_summary`), so it cannot disagree with the request it
describes - an agent-written summary naming a different card from the one
`body` would actually cast is exactly the failure that shape invites.

`reasoning` is the half that *is* the agent's own words, and the half the
human actually reads before deciding. Required and non-blank: a proposal
with no argument for it is a button, not advice.
AdviceIn.title: AdviceIn

AdviceResponse.description:
`POST .../advice`'s answer. No state view: recording a proposal
mutates no `Game`, so there is nothing about the board it could have
changed - the same reason `DeclarePlanResponse` carries none.
AdviceResponse.title: AdviceResponse

Affordability.description:
Whether an action's cost could be paid right now - reported
*alongside* legality, never used to decide it. CR 118.6: "Attempting to
cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action that has an
unpayable cost is a legal action." Casting with no red mana in play is
still casting; this is what tells the difference between "legal and
payable" and "legal and not".
Affordability.title: Affordability

AffordancesResponse.description:
`GET .../affordances/{card_id}` - `affordances.candidates`'s own
`TargetingProfileView` fields plus its candidate list, and (for a cast,
not an ability) the alternative costs and object-cost offers this card
carries right now.
AffordancesResponse.title: AffordancesResponse

AiReviewFailure.description:
One `audit.AI_REVIEW_FAILED_ACTION` row, flattened - `review.py`'s
`_ai_review_failures`. `invoked` separates a reviewer that ran and
failed from one that was never asked at all.
AiReviewFailure.title: AiReviewFailure

AiReviewFailureIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/ai-review-failure` - the durable record
that a post-game AI review could not be produced, and why.

Gated exactly like `AiReviewIn` (post-game only, `uid` must open
`player`'s own seat, and `player` must be a registered AI seat), for the
same reasons: only an AI seat's own driver ever generates a review, so
only it can report that one failed.

`invoked` is the field this shape exists for. Without it "the reviewer
failed" and "the reviewer was never invoked" are the same absence, which
is precisely the ambiguity the pod logs left - it is `True` only when the
wrapper's `/v1/review` was actually reached and answered.
AiReviewFailureIn.title: AiReviewFailureIn

AiReviewFailureResponse.description:
`POST .../ai-review-failure`'s answer, shaped like
`AiReviewResponse`: this mutates no `Game` either.
AiReviewFailureResponse.title: AiReviewFailureResponse

AiReviewIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/ai-review` - the post-game AI review
(`audit.AI_REVIEW_ACTION`), a separate critique generated on Opus from a
seat's own reflection plus the game's review record
(`mtg_agent.driver.review`), never a seat's own account of what it did.

Shaped mostly like `ReflectionIn` and gated the same way (post-game
only, `uid` must open `player`'s own seat) - see that class's docstring
for why the review itself stays one block of text, nothing structured.

**`turning_points`, DR3 owner addon 2, is the one deliberately
structured field.** `mtg_agent.driver.review.parse_turning_points` pulls
it out of the reviewer's own `turning_points: {...}` line so the game's
turning points are stored on the review record as data
(`{<seat>: [{"turn": ..., "action": ..., "why": ...}, ...]}`), not only
argued in `text`'s own prose. Defaulted to `{}` rather than required: a
review whose text carried no parseable line still files.
AiReviewIn.title: AiReviewIn

AiReviewResponse.description:
`POST .../ai-review`'s answer. No state view, for the same reason
`ReflectionResponse` has none: this mutates no `Game`.
AiReviewResponse.title: AiReviewResponse

AlternativeCostView.description:
One CR 118.9 alternative cost this card could be cast under
(`affordances.alternative_costs`), available or not.
AlternativeCostView.title: AlternativeCostView

BlockedCastView.description:
One `LegalActionsResponse.not_now` row - the engine's own
`models.action.BlockedCast`, `model_dump(mode="json")`-ed unchanged.
`zone`/`spell_face` are plain strings on the wire (the engine's `Zone`
enum and `str | None` respectively, already JSON-safe from that dump).
BlockedCastView.title: BlockedCastView

CandidateView.description:
One object `affordances.candidates` found legal for at least one of
an announcement's targeting requirements (`affordances._label` plus
which requirement slots it fills).
CandidateView.title: CandidateView

Card.description:
A card as the rules see it, modern frame era onward.

Immutable once loaded - a printing does not change - `frozen=True` makes
that a pydantic guarantee rather than a convention nobody checks, and
it is not just documentation: `machines/abilities.parse_abilities` and
`machines/triggers.activated_abilities_of` memoise their parse of a
printing's oracle text keyed on `Card.id`, on the strength of this being
true. A `Card` that could still be mutated after construction would make
that cache wrong the moment anything did, silently - see
`tests/test_card.py::test_card_is_immutable`.
Card.title: Card

CardFace.description: One face of a multifaced card.
CardFace.title: CardFace

CardFaceView.description: One face of a double-faced card (`serialize._faces_view`), as printed.
CardFaceView.title: CardFaceView

CardView.description:
One card or permanent, wherever it sits (`serialize._card_view`).

Almost everything past the first eight fields is `| None`, and that is
not laxness: `visibility._redact_facedown_card` replaces a face-down
exile/battlefield card's view with a stub carrying only `id`, `zone`,
`controller`, `owner`, `tapped`, `face_up`, `name` (`"a face-down card"`),
`card_name` (`None`) and `exile_pile` - every other key is simply absent
from that dict. A required field here would make FastAPI's own response
validation fail on exactly the redaction this api exists to perform.
CardView.title: CardView

CastHintsView.description:
What casting this hand/exile card asks for - X, modes, targets, the
faces it may be cast as, and the optional additional costs it may be
announced with (`affordances.cast_hints`).
CastHintsView.title: CastHintsView

CastOptionView.description:
One CR 601.2b keyword a hand, graveyard or exile card can be cast with
right now (`serialize._cast_option_view`).

From a graveyard or exile it is a CR 601.3 permission to cast the card
from where it sits at all - flashback, mayhem, plot, foretell, madness,
airbend, a printed CR 604.6 zone permission, or a keyword granted by
another permanent's static ability. From the hand it is a bare CR 118.9
alternative cost that replaces the printed mana cost, which is evoke,
dash, morph, megamorph, disguise, bestow and warp's hand half.

`usable_now` is the option's own answer (`KeywordCastOption.why_not`:
zone, marker owner and turn, "discarded this turn", a keyword's own "as a
sorcery" clause) and never CR 117.1a's timing rule for the card itself -
`GET .../legal-actions` is what answers "could I do this right now".
CastOptionView.title: CastOptionView

ChoiceView.description:
CR 614.12a's "as this enters, choose ..." answer
(`serialize._card_view`'s `choice` key, from `models.card_state.Choice`).
ChoiceView.title: ChoiceView

ConcedeRequest.description:
CR 104.3a: a player may concede at any time, and leaves the game
immediately. No priority is required and nothing can refuse it, so unlike
every other action request this one has no `dry_run` - there is nothing to
ask permission for.
ConcedeRequest.title: ConcedeRequest

ConcedeResponse.description:
`POST .../actions/concede` - its own shape (CR 104.3a: nothing can
refuse a concession, so this never carries `reason`), not
`_respond`/`ActionOutcome`.
ConcedeResponse.title: ConcedeResponse

ContentsCardView.description:
A card view with no `id` (`serialize._contents_view` never sets one) -
a contents entry names no single object, because naming one would pin it
to a place in an unordered zone.
ContentsCardView.title: ContentsCardView

ContentsEntryView.description:
One entry of `library_contents`/`sideboard_contents`: identical cards
counted together, with no id and no position (CR 401.2).
ContentsEntryView.title: ContentsEntryView

ConvokeChoice.description:
One creature tapped to pay one symbol of a convoke spell's cost.

CR 702.51b: convoke "isn't an additional or alternative cost and applies
only after the total cost of the spell with convoke is determined", so
this is not part of the announcement - it is which objects the payer
offers against the already-determined cost.
ConvokeChoice.title: ConvokeChoice

CrewRequest.description:
CR 702.122a: "Crew N" means "Tap any number of other untapped
creatures you control with total power N or greater: This permanent
becomes an artifact creature until end of turn."

Crew is an activated ability of the Vehicle, not of the creatures, and it
has no `{T}` symbol of its own - so this is not an `ActivateRequest`
against an ability index. The creatures are the cost.
CrewRequest.title: CrewRequest

CycleRequest.description:
CR 702.29a: "[Cost], Discard this card: Draw a card." An activated
ability, but one `Game.begin_activating`/`activate_ability` cannot reach -
they only ever activate a battlefield permanent's ability, and cycling
"functions only while the card... is in a player's hand" (CR 702.29b) - so
it gets its own request shape and endpoint rather than reusing
`ActivateRequest`.
CycleRequest.title: CycleRequest

CyclingEntry.description:
One cycling ability this hand card can activate right now
(`serialize._special_actions`'s `cycling` list).
CyclingEntry.title: CyclingEntry

DamageAssignmentRequest.description:
One `(target, amount)` entry for the `assign_combat_damage` kind's
`decide` answer (CR 510.1c, CR 702.19b) - the request-side twin of the
engine's `machines.decisions.DamageAssignment`.

`target` is a card id (a blocker, from `pending_decision.cards[1:]`) or a
player's username (the defending player or planeswalker, offered only
once every blocker has been assigned its own `pending_decision
.lethal_damage` and only when `pending_decision.trample` is true) - the
same "card id or player name" token shape `DeclaredPairRequest.defender`
already uses, told apart the same way (`decisions.damage_answer`).
DamageAssignmentRequest.title: DamageAssignmentRequest

DecideResponse.description:
`POST .../decide` - its own `accepted`/`reason` shape, not
`allowed`/`ActionOutcome`: `decide` answers a standing question rather
than attempting a new action, so "was this answer accepted" is the
question, not "was this allowed".
DecideResponse.title: DecideResponse

DecisionAbilityView.description:
One `card_details` entry naming an ability rather than a card -
`decisions.PendingDecision.abilities`' own shape (`ORDER_TRIGGERS`,
CR 603.3b) and `serialize._stack_view`'s ability entry (a `CHOOSE_TARGETS`
aimed at an ability on the stack, CR 115.2) both validate as this, since
an ability "can be an activated or triggered ability on the stack. This
kind of ability is an object" (CR 113.1c) with no card of its own behind
it to name it by.

`source_card_id` is the permanent the trigger came from
(`machines.decisions.PendingAbility.source_id`) - what lets a client
point at that permanent on the board, and tell two copies of one card
apart, which the source name alone cannot. `zone` is `None` for an
`ORDER_TRIGGERS` entry: CR 603.3b is asked one step *before* CR 603.3's
"its controller puts it on the stack", so at the moment this entry is
published the ability is in no zone at all - `"stack"` only once
`serialize._stack_view` is the one publishing it, after it has actually
been placed there.
DecisionAbilityView.title: DecisionAbilityView

DeckSupportClause.description:
One clause of a `DeckSupportWarning`'s card - `magic_cards_model.
support.SupportClause`'s own `text`/`outcome`/`reason`, carried verbatim
rather than the whole clause (`kind`/`status`/`source` are the engine's
own bookkeeping, not something a decklist owner needs to see). Only a
clause that is not itself `handled` is ever included here - see
`decks._support_warning_for`.
DeckSupportClause.title: DeckSupportClause

DeckSupportWarning.description:
One card the engine does not fully support, as flow 6 (W2) surfaces
it on every decklist submit/validate/load: `magic_cards_model.support.
card_support`'s own verdict for the card, sourced never hard-coded.
`unaudited` is one of `docs/engine-coverage.md`'s own four-tier ladder -
a static ability nothing has checked either way, as opposed to `silent`
(nothing reads the clause at all) or `notice` (read, but fails closed on
purpose) - but every non-`handled` status here is treated the same way:
likely not working, never a softer tier a caller can afford to ignore.
A fully `handled` card never appears; `decks.deck_support_warnings` is
what builds this list.
DeckSupportWarning.title: DeckSupportWarning

DeclarePlanIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/plan` - a seat's declaration, made before
it acts, of how it reads this turn.

Five fields and no more, but three of them are now cheaper to write
(F3, MEMORY.md dated): `board_read` and `my_role` are objective/stable
enough that a seat should not have to retype them every turn, and a plan
that still holds should not have to be re-composed from scratch. What
never gets cheaper is `prediction` - the part of a declaration that is
actually evidence, checkable against what the opponent then did.

`uid` is the seat's own credential, carried in the body beside `player`
rather than in the query string: a plan is hidden information about how
a seat intends to play, so the server checks that the caller *is* the
seat it is declaring for before writing anything into its name.
DeclarePlanIn.title: DeclarePlanIn

DeclarePlanResponse.description:
`POST .../plan`'s answer. No state view: a declaration mutates no
`Game`, so there is nothing about the board that this could have
changed.
DeclarePlanResponse.title: DeclarePlanResponse

DeclaredPairRequest.description:
One `(creature, defender)` pair for the `declare_attackers`/
`declare_blockers` kinds' `decide` answer (CR 508.1, CR 509.1) - the
request-side twin of the engine's `machines.decisions.DeclaredPair`.

`defender` is a card id (UUID string) or a player's username, the same
token shape `CastRequest.targets`/`ActivateRequest.targets`/
`DecideRequest.targets` already use for "a card or a player" - told apart
the same way (`decisions.declared_pairs_answer`). A blocker always blocks
a creature (CR 509.1a), so `defender` is a card id for every
`declare_blockers` pair; an attacker's defender is overwhelmingly a
player (CR 508.1b) but can also be a planeswalker or a battle's card id.
DeclaredPairRequest.title: DeclaredPairRequest

DivisionView.description:
CR 601.2d's divided-effect shape (`affordances._profile_view`'s
`division`) - Electrolyze's damage, distributed counters.
DivisionView.title: DivisionView

EquipRequest.description:
CR 702.6a: "Equip [cost]" means "[Cost]: Attach this permanent to
target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery."

A keyword ability the engine builds on its own (`machines.keywords.
equip_activation`) rather than one of the Equipment's
`activated_abilities`, so there is no ability index to name - the same
reason crew and cycling have their own request shapes.
EquipRequest.title: EquipRequest

ExilePileView.description:
CR 406.4's pile marker (`serialize._exile_pile`) - which special
action put this card in exile, whose it is, and the turn it landed.
ExilePileView.title: ExilePileView

GameLogResponse.description:
`GET .../log`'s response. `log` entries are left as `dict[str, Any]`
deliberately: `audit.entries`' `detail` payload is exactly as
per-action-shaped as `ActionOutcome`'s own extra fields (T10's
`audit.record(**keys)` writes whatever the calling route passed), and a
log entry additionally carries an optional full board `snapshot`
(`serialize.snapshot`) - modelling either faithfully is a second task's
worth of work this one does not need, since neither is one of the four
components T1 requires by name (the request models, `PendingDecision`,
the state view, the outcome shape).
GameLogResponse.title: GameLogResponse

GameStateView.description:
The full board (`serialize.state_view`), as a viewer may see it after
`visibility.redact_view` - see this section's own module-level note for
why so much of this is `| None`. `libraries`/`sideboards` are the two
fields redaction removes outright rather than merely emptying (CR 401.2:
nobody may look at a library, not even their own); `you` is the one field
`redact_view` *adds* that `state_view` itself never sets.
GameStateView.title: GameStateView

GameSummaryScalars.description:
One game's row from `GET /api/games/summary` (2b's T8, map's S2) -
exactly the scalars a lobby list needs and nothing a full `state_view`
would cost to build: no card views, no Scryfall images, one bulk call
for every id a poll asks about instead of one `state_view` per game.
GameSummaryScalars.title: GameSummaryScalars

HypotheticalFactsResponse.description:
`GET .../playscripts/hypothetical-facts`'s response
(`hypothetical_facts.build_hypothetical_facts`) - O4/O7's engine-computed
per-card facts, keyed by card id (a string: JSON has no UUID keys).
`cards[id]` is `{"enters"?: str, "unlocks"?: bool,
"unlocks_by_search"?: bool, "unlocks_by_basic_search"?: bool,
"payable_any"?: str, "unlocks_next"?: bool}` - only the facts that card
actually has, the same shape `selectors.Hypo` reads. The last two
(T5) reach the response only when the request named `?horizon=next_turn`
(T4, `app.get_hypothetical_facts`); with no horizon, this is byte for
byte what it always was. `notices` is every notice the engine
raised while working any of them out (an unread enters-tapped line, a
lethal optional payment, an unresolved trigger); it is not tied to one
card, since `selectors.matches` already applies the "any notice fails
`unlocks` closed" rule per pair before this response is built - it is
here for a caller that wants to see why.
HypotheticalFactsResponse.title: HypotheticalFactsResponse

KnownCardsView.description:
What one player knows about hidden cards (`Game.known_to`): cards in
another player's hand, library cards with their live position, and
sideboard cards. The player's own hand and sideboard are never listed.
KnownCardsView.title: KnownCardsView

KnownLibraryCardView.description:
One library card a player knows, with where it sits right now
(`serialize._known_cards_view`; CR 701.20d ends it on a reordering).
KnownLibraryCardView.title: KnownLibraryCardView

Layout.description: How the card is arranged. Changes how it is cast and how it behaves in play.
Layout.title: Layout

LegalActionsResponse.description:
`GET .../legal-actions` (T11) - the engine's own `Action` model,
reused as-is rather than re-shaped: `get_legal_actions` returns exactly
`[action.model_dump(mode="json") for action in actions]`, and
`records.LegalActionsBefore.actions` (surfaced redacted, per-viewer, as
`LogEntry.legal_actions_before`) is the identical dump - now with the
legal candidates for each targeting action folded in alongside.

**Both names stay in `#/components/schemas`, and the union is why.**
Typing this `list[ActionWithTargets]` alone read as an enrichment and was
one: every `Action` field is still there, by inheritance. But FastAPI
names a component only where a route references it, and the subclass was
the only thing referenced - so the engine's `Action`, which downstream
repos validate against **by name** (`tests/test_openapi_drift.py`'s own
docstring), silently stopped being published at all. The union restores
it without touching the wire, because it is also the truth about the
answer: `candidates=false` (the default, and what `ui/app.js` asks for)
answers plain engine `Action` rows, and `candidates=true` adds `targets`
to the targeting ones - `_attach_target_candidates` sets that key or
leaves it off, never sets it to null. `targets` being required on the
subclass is what keeps the two branches apart: a row carrying candidates
matches `ActionWithTargets` and only it, a row without matches `Action`
and only it, so neither branch is decoration and a client can tell which
it is holding by the one key that differs.
LegalActionsResponse.title: LegalActionsResponse

Legalities.description:
Clamped to the three rotating-to-modern constructed formats.

Scryfall's other formats (legacy, vintage, commander, pauper, the Arena-only
ones) are dropped by the `extra="ignore"` config.
Legalities.title: Legalities

LoyaltyHintView.description:
CR 606.2's loyalty symbol (`affordances.ability_hints`'s `loyalty`
key) - present only for a loyalty ability.
LoyaltyHintView.title: LoyaltyHintView

ManualManaStepView.description:
One mana ability to activate by hand before a cast row is payable
(`ActionRow.activate_first`) - `POST .../actions/activate` with these
`card_id`/`ability_index` (and `color`, when present).
ManualManaStepView.title: ManualManaStepView

MintSeatRequest.description:
2b's T8, the seat back door's mint half. `player` must already be
registered on the game (`Game.players`) - this mints a fresh credential
for an existing seat, it does not add a player to the game.
MintSeatRequest.title: MintSeatRequest

ModalHintsView.description:
CR 700.2's modal shape (`affordances.cast_hints`'s `modes` key) -
present only for a modal card.
ModalHintsView.title: ModalHintsView

MoveCardSuccessResponse.description:
`move_card`'s response when the move was allowed:
`{**state_view(...), **outcome.body()}` plus `log_seq`. When the move was
refused, `move_card` returns bare `ActionOutcome` instead - no state at
all - so the route's real response type is
`ActionOutcome | MoveCardSuccessResponse`, not this model alone.
MoveCardSuccessResponse.title: MoveCardSuccessResponse

MulliganRequest.description:
One seat's CR 103.5 declaration: "a player who is dissatisfied with
their initial hand may take a mulligan".

`BoardRead` because this is a mutating move a seat makes and records
(`mulligan_declared`, one of `scripts/eval_report.py`'s `PLAY_ACTIONS`),
so a refusal of it belongs in the same measured split as every other:
without an `expected_seq` to name, a seat's first declaration of the game
was the one move whose refusals could not be told apart from a lost race.
Optional here exactly as it is everywhere else - the browser names no
board and is refused on nothing new.
MulliganRequest.title: MulliganRequest

NewGameResponse.description:
`POST /api/games`'s own response - the full, unredacted state view
(the creator gets every seat's uid and the admin key in one call, so a
filtered view would hide nothing a redaction step is for) plus the seat
credentials themselves.
NewGameResponse.title: NewGameResponse

ObjectCostCandidateView.description:
One object offered against a cost that is paid with objects rather
than mana - convoke/delve/crew (`affordances.object_costs`'s `eligible()`)
or an alternative cost's own `choosing`
(`affordances._alternative_cost_candidates`). `CandidateView`'s shape
minus `requirements` (this is a payment offer, not a targeting slot) plus
an optional `power`, present only for a battlefield candidate, and an
optional `pays`, present only on an alternative cost's candidates.
ObjectCostCandidateView.title: ObjectCostCandidateView

ObjectCostHintView.description:
One way this card's cost may be paid with objects rather than mana -
convoke (CR 702.51a), delve (CR 702.66a) or improvise (CR 702.126a), as
`affordances.cast_hints` reads them off the printing.

The printed half only: *which* creatures, graveyard cards or artifacts
qualify needs a board, and is `object_costs` on
`GET .../affordances/{card_id}`. This rides the card view for the same
reason `additional_costs` does - it is what a client holds the moment the
card is picked up, before any affordance fetch, and a cost not known that
early is one the client cannot stop the cast for. Kappa Cannoneer is the
case that proved it: no targets, no X, no modes, so the browser fired the
cast at its full {5}{U} with the artifact-tap step never offered.
ObjectCostHintView.title: ObjectCostHintView

ObjectCostsView.description:
Which objects could be spent on this card's cost, and for what
(`affordances.object_costs`) - only the keys that apply are ever
present.
ObjectCostsView.title: ObjectCostsView

OpeningHandActionRequest.description:
One CR 103.6 action with a card in this seat's own opening hand -
"some cards allow a player to take actions with them from their opening
hand".
OpeningHandActionRequest.title: OpeningHandActionRequest

OpeningHandFinishResponse.description:
`POST .../pregame/opening-hand/finish` (`opening.finish_opening_hand_actions`,
settled through any priorityless step by `app._settled`).
OpeningHandFinishResponse.title: OpeningHandFinishResponse

OpeningHandOptionView.description:
One CR 103.6 action a seat's own opening hand offers right now
(`opening.pregame_view`'s `opening_hand_options` entries).
OpeningHandOptionView.title: OpeningHandOptionView

OpponentPrediction.description:
What a seat expects its opponent to do next, and why.

The prediction is the part of a declaration that makes it evidence
rather than commentary: it is checkable against what the opponent then
actually did, and `review.py` puts the two side by side without grading
either. `because` is required for the same reason - a call with no read
behind it is a guess, and a guess that happens to land proves nothing.
OpponentPrediction.title: OpponentPrediction

OptionalCostChoice.description:
One optional cost a cast pays (`CastRequest.optional_costs`).

`keyword` is the cost's own keyword, case-insensitively: `Kicker` and
`Multikicker` (CR 702.33a/c, `Casting.pay_kicker`), `Replicate`
(CR 702.56a, `Casting.pay_replicate`), `Offspring` (CR 702.175a,
`Casting.pay_offspring`), `Blight` (CR 701.68a's "you may blight N",
`Casting.pay_blight`), `Gift` (CR 702.174a, `Casting.pay_gift`),
`Entwine` (CR 702.42a, `Casting.choose_modes(entwined=True)` - name every
mode in `modes` too), `Escalate` (CR 702.120a, `Casting.pay_escalate` -
charged for every mode beyond the first whether or not it is named; name
it to hand over the objects a non-mana escalate cost takes) and
`Harmonize` (CR 702.180a/b, `Casting.pay_harmonize` - the creature a
`keyword: Harmonize` cast taps to reduce its cost) and `Pay life`
(CR 601.2b, the life half of a "pay N life or pay {M}" additional cost,
`Casting.paying_life_for_additional_cost`) - every optional cost choice
the engine charges.
OptionalCostChoice.title: OptionalCostChoice

OptionalCostView.description:
One optional additional cost a cast row's card offers (CR 118.8) -
`action_rows.legal_action_rows`. Its `keyword` is what
`CastRequest.optional_costs[].keyword` takes back.
OptionalCostView.title: OptionalCostView

PassPriorityResponse.description:
`POST .../actions/pass-priority`'s own shape - never merges the state
view (unlike `advance`, which moves the turn marker, passing priority
only ever resolves the stack's top or ends the step).
PassPriorityResponse.title: PassPriorityResponse

PendingDecisionView.description:
The question a paused command is waiting on (`decisions.PendingDecision
.to_view`), or - for any viewer but the deciding player and the admin -
`visibility.redact_pending_decision`'s `{player, kind, prompt}` shrink of
it (CR 101.4a: a choice made in a hidden zone stays face down for
everyone else). Every field past `prompt` is `| None` for that reason,
not because the engine ever leaves them unset for the deciding player.

Named `PendingDecisionView` rather than `PendingDecision`: that name is
already the (non-pydantic) dataclass in `decisions.py` this view mirrors,
and the two are not interchangeable - `decisions.PendingDecision` also
knows how to build itself `from_engine`, which is no part of a response
contract.
PendingDecisionView.title: PendingDecisionView

PlayPermissionView.description: One live CR 601.3 dynamic cast/play grant (`serialize._play_permission_view`).
PlayPermissionView.title: PlayPermissionView

PlayerView.description:
One seat's own block (`serialize._player_view`). No `decklist` or
`agent` field any more (2b's T8, map's S6): both were lobby-owned state
read here on every state poll, the hot reverse seam the six-way cut
cannot carry. Both moved to the lobby's own
`GET /api/lobby/games/{id}/seats` (`decks_api.SeatDetail`), `decklist`
redacted there per-viewer the same way it used to be redacted here - see
`serialize._player_view`'s own docstring.
PlayerView.title: PlayerView

PlaysOutcomeAdmitted.description:
One `plays admit` of the handover that landed: its commit on
mtg-decks main and whether it was a DSL change (a play added, deleted,
or changed beyond its `priority`), as the results journal recorded it.

`added`/`updated`/`reprioritized` (DR2) are the same three play-id lists
`admit._Landing` already classifies one admit's own git diff into - a
play file added, one changed beyond its `priority` (or deleted, which
`_Landing` also files under `updated`), or one whose only change was its
`priority`. Optional and empty by default, so a body posted before this
field existed still validates; `playscripts.stats.game_play_stats` is
what turns them, across every `plays_outcome` row of a game, into a
seat's own `play_stats`.
PlaysOutcomeAdmitted.title: PlaysOutcomeAdmitted

PlaysOutcomeIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/plays-outcome` - the driver's record of
what one handover did to the DSL (`audit.PLAYS_OUTCOME_ACTION`), built
from the guides clone's results journal after the handover turn.

Gated like `AiReviewIn`: post-game only, and `uid` must be `player`'s own
credential - an AI seat's own seat uid (`role: seat`), or an advisor uid
for the human it watches (`role: advisor`). Never a controlled player's:
CR 723.5 hands a controller in-game decisions, not the post-game record.

`state` is `complete` when the handover landed a DSL change or a
no-change for every candidate, and `unfinished` otherwise, with
`unfinished_reasons` saying why (nudged, timed out, an admit or propose
that did not succeed, a re-push that did not satisfy). `repushed` says
the one re-push turn ran; `followup` that this row comes from the
follow-up DSL-development Job rather than the handover itself.

An `unfinished` row that is not a follow-up's own schedules F1's one
follow-up Job for this (game, uid) in kubernetes mode
(`lobby.schedule_followup`); `deck` and `opponent` are what that Job's
assignment is built from, so they ride in the row.
PlaysOutcomeIn.title: PlaysOutcomeIn

PlaysOutcomeNoChange.description:
One `plays no-change`: the candidate (a play id or a hand-played
line) and why it needs no DSL change.
PlaysOutcomeNoChange.title: PlaysOutcomeNoChange

PlaysOutcomeOpponent.description:
The revealed opponent as the driver identified it post-game (A2):
the guided deck's `slug` when there is one, the `archetype` the list
resolved to, and how sure the classifier was. What F1's follow-up is
handed when the opponent's list is no longer readable.
PlaysOutcomeOpponent.title: PlaysOutcomeOpponent

PlaysOutcomeProposed.description:
One `guides propose` of the handover: the commit it landed (`sha`),
or, when it landed nothing, its result (`conflict`, `refused`, ...).
PlaysOutcomeProposed.title: PlaysOutcomeProposed

PlaysOutcomeResponse.description:
`POST .../plays-outcome`'s answer, shaped like `AiReviewResponse`:
this mutates no `Game` either.
PlaysOutcomeResponse.title: PlaysOutcomeResponse

PregameSettleRequest.description:
Admin-only: run the whole pregame (CR 103.5's mulligan process, CR
103.6's opening-hand actions) forward, all at once, over every seat.

`BoardRead` for the same reason every other mutating request carries it:
this is a command like any other (`commands._run_pregame_settle`), it
reaches the same `records.legal_actions_before` sites, and an operator
settling a pregame against a board that has since moved is owed the news
that it moved rather than a settled game they did not ask for.
PregameSettleRequest.title: PregameSettleRequest

PregameSettleResponse.description:
`POST .../pregame/settle` - always the full state view, both paused
and completed (admin-only, T7b).
PregameSettleResponse.title: PregameSettleResponse

PregameStallView.description:
One pregame obligation the game is held on: a move owed by a seat
nothing is playing, that `ai_pregame.py`'s backstop refused to answer
because the answer would have been a choice rather than a forced move.
See `ai_pregame.is_forced` and `ai_pregame.stall_text`.
PregameStallView.title: PregameStallView

PregameView.description:
What the game is waiting for in the pregame (`opening.pregame_view`),
or `None` once CR 103.8's first turn has begun. `opening_hand_options`
names cards in a hidden zone (CR 402.3), so `visibility._redact_pregame`
empties every seat's entry but the viewer's own - never removes the key,
so this needs no `| None` of its own beyond the whole field on
`GameStateView`.
PregameView.title: PregameView

ReflectionIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/reflection` - a seat's own post-game
write-up, filed once the result is already known.

Deliberately the only shape this ever takes: one seat, one block of
free text. Unlike `DeclarePlanIn`'s five structured fields, there is
nothing here a post-game review has to show and cannot reconstruct from
the board - the whole point of a reflection is that it is the agent's
own words, in its own shape, written after the game rather than during
it. Splitting it into board-read/plan/prediction fields the way a
declaration is split would dress up a narrative as evidence it never
was; `review.py`'s reflection section already says in words that
nothing here is evidence of anything the review pairs above it.

`uid` mirrors `DeclarePlanIn.uid`: the seat's own credential, carried in
the body, so nobody may write a reflection into another seat's name.
ReflectionIn.title: ReflectionIn

ReflectionResponse.description:
`POST .../reflection`'s answer. No state view, for the same reason
`DeclarePlanResponse` has none: a reflection mutates no `Game`.
ReflectionResponse.title: ReflectionResponse

RelatedCard.description: A card this one is closely related to - a token, meld part, or combo piece.
RelatedCard.title: RelatedCard

ResolveTopResponse.description:
`POST .../resolve-top` - always the full state view. `reason` is set
(with `resolved: None`) when `engine_api.resolve_top` itself refused
(no legal object to resolve), which is still a `RunStatus.COMPLETED`
result, not a paused or a raised one.
ResolveTopResponse.title: ResolveTopResponse

RestrictedManaView.description:
How much of a pool carries one particular CR 106.6 restriction
(`models.mana.RestrictedMana`).

`amounts` is a **subset** of `ManaPoolView.floating`, never a replacement
for it: CR 106.4a has the player announce all the mana that is there, and
the restriction narrows only what may be done with it. Without the amount
two restricted `{C}` and two plain `{C}` are one `floating {"C": 2}` and
nothing tells them apart.
RestrictedManaView.title: RestrictedManaView

RestrictionView.description:
A CR 106.6 "Spend this mana only to ..." sentence, as a seat sees it.

`text` is the printed sentence verbatim, so a refusal quotes the card
rather than the parser's reading of it.

`understood` is whether the engine turned that sentence into anything it
can check. **False is not cosmetic and is never hidden**: an unread
restriction is fail-closed in the engine - the mana exists, is announced
(CR 106.4a), empties with the pool, and pays for nothing at all - so a view
that showed the mana without this flag would be telling the player they
have a resource they cannot spend.

Deliberately two fields and no third: the engine's own `SpendClause` tuple
is the parser's internal shape and is still being changed underneath, so
publishing it here would pin it.
RestrictionView.title: RestrictionView

ReviewAdvice.description:
One `audit.ADVICE_ACTION` row - the mtg-buddy advisor's own proposal
to a human seat - paired with whether it was approved and what the seat
did about it (`review.py`'s `_advice`).

A stream of its own, beside `declarations` rather than folded into it: a
declaration's window runs from one `plan_declared` row to the next *by
any seat*; an advice row is per-decision-point and would fragment that
window if it were treated as a second kind of marker. It is not - see
`_advice`'s own docstring.

Nothing here grades the advice either, for the same reason
`ReviewDeclaration` grades no prediction: whether it was *good* is a
judgement, not an outcome. What is reported is one of four things:
approved and followed; approved, attempted, and refused by the engine
(`did` is `None` - a refusal is a failed attempt, never the outcome -
but `refused` carries the row and the engine's own verbatim reason, so
nothing is lost); never approved and the seat did something else (`did`
is that row); or never approved and the seat did nothing before the next
piece of advice (`did` is `None`, `refused` is empty).

`approved` and `followed` are independent, and the pair a reader is most
often after is `approved: true, followed: false` - the seat agreed to
this and then did something else. That takes BOTH fields to see: `did`
alone cannot say it, and `approved` alone cannot either.
ReviewAdvice.title: ReviewAdvice

ReviewDecision.description:
One committing row of one seat's own ledger, converted to the
play-script DSL (DR2, `playscripts.decision_dsl.decision_rows`) - a cast,
an activation, a land play, an answer to a pending decision, a combat
declaration, a mulligan, an opening-hand action, a priority pass, or a
script run it started.

`dsl` is that decision written as a schema-valid `Play`, or `None` when
the DSL vocabulary cannot say it at all - `unexpressible` then names why,
and exactly one of the two fields is ever `None`. `board` is the compact,
card-name-free board (`decision_dsl.compact_board`) built from this
row's own recorded exact state (`GET .../review/frames/{seq}`'s own
shape) - `None` for a row with no state recorded, never a board from
another `seq`. `board_by_perspective` (the 2026-09-24 owner addon) is
two such boards, one per player, each independently redacted through
`visibility.redact_view` to what that player could actually see at this
exact moment: `hand` is that player's own hand card names,
`known_opponent_hand` is whatever of the opponent's hand this player was
specifically shown or looked at by then (`known_cards`), and
`known_library` is whatever specific library card - anyone's, including
this player's own - this player had looked at or been shown by then
(CR 701.20a/e, a scry or a look at the top of a library being the
canonical case), in the order those cards sit. Never the opponent's
hidden cards otherwise, and never a library's full *contents* or order
for anyone, including its own owner - only the specific cards this
player actually knows. `None` for the same rows `board` is `None` for.
ReviewDecision.title: ReviewDecision

ReviewDeclaration.description:
One `plan_declared` row, paired with what happened next.

Nothing on this model grades the prediction - no score, no hit flag, no
verdict. See `review.py` for why the raw pairing is the thing a sceptic
cannot argue with.
ReviewDeclaration.title: ReviewDeclaration

ReviewEntry.description:
One ledger row as a declaration's pairing carries it - no `snapshot`,
which lives once in `GameReviewResponse.entries` (see `review.py`).
ReviewEntry.title: ReviewEntry

ReviewPlayStats.description:
One seat's per-game play-script statistics (DR2,
`playscripts.stats.game_play_stats`): its registered corpus size, split
move-bearing/advice-only; how many script offers it saw and what became
of them (`used`/`denied`/`passed_over`, out of `offered`); and, across
every `plays_outcome` row of this game, the distinct play ids its
handovers admitted as `added`/`updated`/`reprioritized`.
ReviewPlayStats.title: ReviewPlayStats

ScriptRunIn.description:
`POST /api/games/{game_id}/script-runs` - one script run, reported by
the runner at its `start` and again at its `finish`, or one offer of a
play the runner never ran (`phase: offer`).

Not a game action: it mutates no `Game`, and the moves a script makes go
through the action routes, which gate them. So none of
`records.require_current_board`, `require_reasoning` or `require_plan`
applies, and there is no `expected_seq` or `reasoning` here to read.

`start` is refused with `code: unknown_script` when `script_id` is not
in the corpus registered under the uid that runs it, and with exit
`already_ran` when this `seat` already started (or finished) `script_id`
at this `turn` and `step`. `finish`
writes one `script_run` row carrying every field below.
ScriptRunIn.title: ScriptRunIn

ScriptsCorpusResponse.description:
`GET .../seats/{uid}/scripts` - the registered corpus, readable by that
uid, the seat's advisor and the admin key only.
ScriptsCorpusResponse.title: ScriptsCorpusResponse

ScriptsRegisterIn.description:
`PUT /api/games/{game_id}/seats/{uid}/scripts` - the play-script corpus
a seat Job runs, registered under the uid it runs with.

`scripts` is deliberately a list of plain objects here rather than
`playscripts.schema.Play`: every script is judged by
`playscripts.schema.play_errors`, which answers with the coded errors
(`unknown-field`, `forbidden-kind`, ...) mtg-decks' own checker shares,
and a refusal the runner can act on is worth more than pydantic's
generic 422. The shape each must satisfy is
`contract/playscript.schema.json`.
ScriptsRegisterIn.title: ScriptsRegisterIn

ScriptsRegisteredResponse.description:
`PUT .../seats/{uid}/scripts`'s answer. The corpus itself is not echoed
back; `GET` of the same path reads it.
ScriptsRegisteredResponse.title: ScriptsRegisteredResponse

SeatLookupResponse.description:
2b's T8, the seat back door's lookup half: `GET /api/seats/{uid}`
resolves a uid to its game with no game id known in advance - the
capability `store.seat_uids` gave an in-process caller for free and no
out-of-process one (a test, or a shared mcp server, M2) can reach.
SeatLookupResponse.title: SeatLookupResponse

SetStepResponse.description:
`PUT .../step`'s response - the harness teleport, always just the
board: it moves the raw turn marker (`engine_api.set_step`,
`Game.advance_to`) rather than running `Game.advance`'s own
beginning-of-step turn-based actions and triggers, so there is nothing
beyond `GameStateView` for it to carry.
SetStepResponse.title: SetStepResponse

SpecialActionEntry.description:
One of `suspend`/`plot`/`foretell`'s current cost, if this hand card
can take that action right now (`serialize._special_actions`).
SpecialActionEntry.title: SpecialActionEntry

SpecialActionRequest.description:
A CR 116.2 special action that exiles a card from hand to cast later:
suspend (CR 116.2f), plot (CR 116.2k), or foretell (CR 116.2h). All three
share this shape - locate the card, pay its special-action cost, exile it
into its own marked pile - so one request body serves all three actions.
SpecialActionRequest.title: SpecialActionRequest

SpecialActionsView.description:
A hand card's live CR 116.2 special actions and cycling
(`serialize._special_actions`). Every field is the "not right now" answer
when absent - the card simply cannot take that action at the moment.
SpecialActionsView.title: SpecialActionsView

SpellFaceHintView.description:
One face a cast of this card may name (CR 709.3's split halves, CR
715.3's Adventure) - `affordances.cast_hints`' own reading of the
engine's `machines/casting.castable_faces`, the same set `legal_actions`
emits one `Action` per.

On the card view rather than only on a row for the reason every other
cast hint is: the hand menu has to offer the halves the moment the player
picks the card up, and a half that is not on screen before the cast is
committed is a half the player never chose. Without it the browser cast
Wear // Tear with no face named at all, which keeps the printing's
combined cost and both halves' targeting.
SpellFaceHintView.title: SpellFaceHintView

SpendEffectManaView.description:
`RestrictedManaView`'s twin for CR 106.6's *other* clause - "have an
additional effect that affects the spell or ability that mana is spent on"
(`models.mana.SpendEffectMana`).

Its own list rather than a permissive restriction, because it narrows
nothing: the mana pays for whatever it could have paid for anyway, and the
sentence only says what happens to the spell it is spent on. So there is no
`understood` half to report - an unread one costs the player nothing.
SpendEffectManaView.title: SpendEffectManaView

SpliceOption.description:
One card in `player`'s hand that could be revealed to splice its text
onto this `CAST` action's spell (CR 702.47a), before any is chosen.

Unlike `spell_face`/`alternative_cost`, this is not one of a family of
mutually exclusive ways to cast the same card - CR 702.47b lets more
than one splice card apply to the same spell at once ("If you're
splicing more than one card onto a spell, reveal them all at once"), so
a `CAST` action carries the whole eligible pool here, the same
"parameter space, not an enumeration" treatment `Action.modes` already
gives a modal spell's bullets. Choosing one (or several) happens on the
in-flight `Casting.splice(name)`, not here.
SpliceOption.title: SpliceOption

StackAbilityView.description:
An activated or triggered ability on the stack (CR 113.1c, CR 603) -
`serialize._stack_view`'s other shape. No `CardView` fields: an ability
is "an object that's not a card" (CR 603.3), so it carries its own
source name and ability text instead.
StackAbilityView.title: StackAbilityView

StackSpellView.description:
A spell on the stack (`serialize._stack_view`) - a `CardView` plus the
`kind` discriminator that tells it apart from `StackAbilityView`.
StackSpellView.title: StackSpellView

StateBasedActionsResponse.description:
`POST .../state-based-actions` - always the full state view, both
paused and completed.
StateBasedActionsResponse.title: StateBasedActionsResponse

TapCardResponse.description:
`POST .../cards/{card_id}/tap` - `audit_outcome` only, no state view
merged in. `tapped` is present only on the success outcome
(`engine_api.Outcome(True, detail={"tapped": ...})`); the refusal branch
(`engine_api.refused(exc)`) carries no detail at all.
TapCardResponse.title: TapCardResponse

TargetRef.description:
One pending-decision candidate or chosen target - a card, a player, or
an ability on the stack named the way a card is (`decisions._target_view`).
No `name`: unlike `TargetRefView` below, this is what a client answers
`POST .../decide` with, not a display value.
TargetRef.title: TargetRef

TargetRefView.description:
One resolved target, with a display name for the UI
(`serialize._target_refs`) - what `CardView.target_refs` and a stack
ability's own `target_refs` carry, as opposed to `TargetRef` above.
TargetRefView.title: TargetRefView

TargetRequirementView.description:
One targeting requirement's shape (`affordances._profile_view`'s
`requirements` entries) - how many targets it wants and, for a modal
card, which mode it belongs to.
TargetRequirementView.title: TargetRequirementView

TargetSlot.description:
One targeting requirement of a cast or an activation (CR 601.2c, and
CR 602.2b for an activation): its phrase, how many targets it takes, and
which objects and players it could legally name right now.

The candidates are ids and usernames only, like `decision_candidates`/
`decision_player_candidates`, and come from the same predicate the
announcement checks with (`TargetRequirement.rejects`), so a candidate
list cannot disagree with what announcing that target would accept. They
are a snapshot of this moment, not a promise: CR 608.2b rechecks on
resolution.
TargetSlot.title: TargetSlot

TargetSlotCandidates.description:
The legal candidates for ONE of an announcement's targeting
requirements (`affordances.target_candidates`), by that requirement's own
index into `Action.target_slots` - so `slot` says which phrase these
answer, and the phrase itself is not repeated here.

`count` is the true total whatever the caps did to `candidates`: a seat
weighing a sweeper needs the number even when it does not need the names,
and a list that quietly shrank while its count shrank with it would be a
list that lies. `truncated` and the absence of `candidates` are the two
ways it can shrink - the per-slot cap (`affordances.CANDIDATE_SLOT_CAP`)
and the whole answer's candidate budget (`mcp.MAX_CANDIDATE_BYTES`).
TargetSlotCandidates.title: TargetSlotCandidates

TargetingProfileView.description:
What an announcement's targeting looks like right now
(`affordances._profile_view`) - shared by `CardView.cast.targeting`,
every `AbilityView.targeting`, and `AffordancesResponse` itself.
TargetingProfileView.title: TargetingProfileView

UnreadableModeView.description:
One mode of a modal spell the engine cannot read into an effect -
`action_rows.legal_action_rows`, from the reading
`effects.resolve_modal_spell` records a `ModeNotice` for.
UnreadableModeView.title: UnreadableModeView

XCostView.description:
What an X cast row is charged at one X its `cost` does not describe
(`action_rows._Rows.with_charged_cost`).
XCostView.title: XCostView

get.description: The decklist files already in the repo, for a picker in the UI.

One bundled decklist's raw text, so the UI can preview or edit it
before starting a game. `name` is resolved strictly inside `DECKS_DIR` -
no `..` escape - since this is a bare filename off a URL path.

Every game this caller may reach.

One row that will not decode must never take this whole route down -
the outage this shape exists for. `store.ids()` names the rows without
decoding any of them; the decode happens here, per game, and a game that
refuses is listed with `unloadable` carrying the decoder's own words
instead of being dropped (a game that vanishes from a list is a worse
lie than a game that says why it cannot be opened) and instead of
raising (which 500'd the listing for every *other* game as well).

2b's T8 (map's S2): the scalars a lobby list needs, for every id in
one call - `ids` comma-separated. Never the full `state_view` per game
`list_lobby_games` used to build just to read four fields back out of
it; unknown ids are silently skipped, the same way that loop already
skipped a `store.get` miss.

A game this caller may not reach (`game_access.can_access_game` -
someone else's owned game) is skipped exactly the same way - not just
unactionable, absent, so a caller cannot even learn *that much* about a
game that is not theirs by asking for its scalars directly.

A game this build cannot *decode* is the one case that is neither
answered nor silently skipped: `serialize.unloadable_game_summary` puts
it in the answer with `unloadable` set. Skipping it here would be worse
than useless - `decks_api.list_lobby_games` reads this route's result to
build the lobby, and a missing row there is exactly how a game the user
played would appear to have vanished.

delete.description:
Delete a game outright. `uid` must be a seat uid of this game, or `key`
this game's admin key - the same guard `decks_api.end_lobby_game` uses,
mirrored here because this route deletes *any* game (not only a
lobby-booted one) and `GET /api/ui/games` publishes every lobby-booted
game's id with no credential required to read the list itself; without
this check, reading the list would be enough to delete a game nobody
handed the caller a seat or an admin key for.

The deletion itself is `lobby.reset_game`, the same release End game
runs, under this route's own audit action - see `lobby.py` for why
deleting without releasing left a watcher polling, a seat process alive,
a registry answering for uids of a game that no longer existed, and (in
`wrapper` mode) a driver that 409s every later dispatch for the life of
its container.

get.description:
The board, filtered to what `uid` may see (`visibility.py`).

`include` is a comma-separated list of extra blocks. The only one is
`contents`: `library_contents` and `sideboard_contents`, the caller's own
library and sideboard as unordered `{card, count}` lists (CR 401.2 keeps
the order from everyone). They are left off by default because the
board is polled constantly and nothing on that path needs them. A value
this route does not know is refused by name rather than ignored.

No uid, or one this game does not recognise, sees nothing hidden - the
same treatment as any other caller talking to the API directly instead
of through a dispatched agent's seat. A valid seat uid sees its own hand
and both public boards; the game's admin key sees everything.

Used to also mark this seat as watching/delivered on the game's decision
mailbox, so a mutating request parked in `Game.ask` could tell a live
seat apart from an unattended one. That whole mechanism is gone - a
mutating request never blocks on a decision any more, so there is
nothing here to be evidence for.

post.description:
Declare attackers (CR 508.1) - see `_answer_declaration`. `dry_run`
answers without touching the pending decision at all: it only checks
each pair's legality (`Game.why_cannot_attack`) against the game as it
stands right now, the same probe it always was - so it needs no `uid`
gate any more than any other dry run does; only a real declaration does.

Cast a card. `dry_run` never asks anything unscripted (it builds and
rewinds its `Casting` against an isolated probe copy of the game - see
`engine_api.dry_run_copy` - never through the pause/resume tape), so it
always completes; a real cast can pause on any CR 601.2 choice this
engine still asks interactively (`choose_targets`, `choose_a_mode`, ...).

Concede (CR 104.3a). A player may do this at any time, and leaves the
game immediately - there is no priority check and nothing to refuse, which
is why this takes no `Outcome` the way the other actions do. `Game.concede`
asks nothing of its own, but this still goes through the pause machinery
like every other command, on the chance a state-based check it triggers
ever does (a legend rule, a leaves-the-battlefield trigger's targets).

Crew a Vehicle (CR 702.122a). Its own endpoint rather than an
`activate` against an ability index: the cost is the creatures tapped,
not mana, and crew is the Vehicle's ability rather than theirs.

CR 702.29a: discard a card with cycling from hand, paying its cycling
cost, to draw a card (or search for a typecycled one). Puts the ability on
the stack, same as `actions/activate` - resolve it with `resolve-top`.
Declare blockers (CR 509.1) - see `_answer_declaration`.

Activate an Equipment's equip ability (CR 702.6a): "[Cost]: Attach this
permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery."

Its own endpoint rather than an `activate` against an ability index, the
same as crew and cycling: equip is a keyword ability the engine builds
(`machines.keywords.equip_activation`), not one of the Equipment's
`activated_abilities`, so there is no index to name. The legal-action row
for it is `kind: equip`.

CR 116.2h/702.143b: pay {2} and exile a card with foretell from hand,
face down. Cast it later with `actions/cast`, `keyword: "Foretell"`, on a
later turn, for its printed foretell cost.

Pass priority - "I am done for now". `outcome` tells the caller what
the pass caused: `resolve_top` (the stack's top resolved, priority goes
round again) or `end_step` (everyone passed on an empty stack, so the
step ended and the next has already begun - CR 117.4, 405.5). Resolving
the stack's top is exactly where a spell or ability's own CR 608.2d
question is asked, so this can pause the same way `resolve-top` can.

If that next step is one in which no player receives priority,
`commands._run_pass_priority` does not stop there: it runs the game on to
the first step somebody can act in (CR 500.3) as part of this same
command, and `settled_through` lists the steps crossed. A player who has
passed has said "I am done for now", and nothing in CR 500.3's untap or
cleanup steps is waiting on them - so handing the pass back with
`priority_holder: null` would be handing back a state no client, human or
otherwise, is allowed to move.

CR 116.2k/702.170b: exile a card with plot from hand, paying its plot
cost. Cast it later with `actions/cast`, `keyword: "Plot"`, on a later turn.

CR 116.2f/702.62a: exile a card with suspend from hand, paying its
suspend cost, with N time counters. The free cast once the last counter
comes off is picked up automatically by `actions/cast` - see `advance`.

Move the turn marker forward. Refused (`allowed: False`) rather than
performed when the stack is non-empty in a step that grants priority
(CR 500.2, 117.4) - the engine's own refusal, not a transport error, so
the caller's next move is `pass-priority`, not a retry - or when the
caller is not the active player or their controller (CR 117.3a, 723.5).

Entering a step whose turn-based action asks something with no scripted
answer - the cleanup discard, CR 508.1's/CR 509.1's combat declarations -
pauses instead of silently defaulting: the committed game is left exactly
as it was (this response's board reflects the step `advance` was called
from, not the one it was trying to enter), with the question attached as
`pending_decision`, answerable through `POST .../decide` or its
`actions/attack`/`actions/declare-blockers` aliases.

schema.title: Response Advance Api Games  Game Id  Advance Post

post.description:
Record one action an advisor thinks `req.player` should take
(`schemas.AdviceIn`), and record nothing else.

**This mutates no `Game`, exactly like `declare_plan`** - which is the
prior art this is modelled on, down to the shape of this docstring. It
calls `audit.record` and nothing else: no `store.replace`, no
compare-and-swap, no version bump. A proposal is a statement *about* the
game, and the whole point of advise mode is that the advisor never moves
it; a route that quietly committed one would hand a read-only credential
the authority its own gate exists to deny.

**The summary is derived here, not taken from the caller.**
`records.advice_summary` reads `req.body` against the live game - card
ids resolved to names, targets and cost spelled out - so what the human
reads can never disagree with the request it describes. `schemas.AdviceIn`
has no `summary` field at all, so an advisor cannot try.

**`based_on_seq` is read immediately before the row is written, under no
lock.** A command landing in between makes this proposal born-stale, and
that is the safe direction: the human's own action carries its own
`expected_seq` (`records.require_current_board`) and is refused against a
board that moved, so a stale proposal costs a refusal rather than a wrong
move. Taking the game's lock here would instead let a buddy pod's
thinking block the seat it is advising.

`legal_actions_before` is computed the same way every acting route
computes it, for `req.player` - what *else* was legal at the moment the
advice was given, which is the comparison a retrospective needs and
cannot reconstruct afterwards. It is hidden information (it names cards
in that player's hand), which is why it rides in the row rather than the
response, and `visibility.redact_log_entry` keeps it - and the whole
proposal - out of the opponent's read of the same log.

Authorised on whoever may already *see* `req.player`'s hand: this game's
advisor for that seat (`visibility.resolve_viewer` resolves an advisor
uid to its human's username), the seat itself, or the admin key. A
proposal names hidden information, so nobody else may write one into that
seat's name - the same rule, and the same 404, `declare_plan` enforces.

`req.drafted_at_seq` (S2 A6) rides straight into `detail` unexamined - it
is a metrics-only marker of when a staged draft was captured, and nothing
here reads it back.

Record that the advised human said yes to the `advice` row at `seq`.

**Mutates no `Game`** - one more `audit.record` call, for the same
reasons `record_advice` above makes none.

**The human's client calls this BEFORE sending the action itself**, and
must not send the action if this fails. That ordering is the whole
purpose of the row: an `advice_approved` row sitting immediately before
the action in the same ledger is what lets a retrospective say "this move
came from the buddy" rather than inferring it from adjacency, and a
refused approval leaves no row at all, so an action taken anyway is
visibly unpaired. (The browser half of that is a later task; the contract
it must honour is pinned by this repo's own tests now, not then.)

**Human uid only, checked twice.** `game_access.py` already refuses an
advisor uid here - this path is neither `/advice` nor `/report`, and the
body claims no `dry_run` - and that is correct and deliberate: an advisor
approving its own advice would make the human's agreement a formality.
This route checks it again itself, against `store.player_for_uid` (a
*seat* credential, never `resolve_viewer`, which an advisor uid passes by
design), because a rule this load-bearing should not rest on one gate
remembering to run.

get.description:
Which objects this announcement could legally target right now.

The expensive half of `affordances.py` - it walks every object in the
public zones against every requirement - so it is asked for on demand,
when the player picks a card up, rather than folded into the 1.2s state
poll for the whole board. The cheap half (does it target, how many, is
there an X, is it modal) already rides along on each card view.

`modes` is a comma-separated list of 1-based mode numbers: a modal
spell's targeting is unanswerable until the modes are chosen (CR 700.2f),
so the UI asks again with them once the player has picked.

`spell_face` is the half being cast, for a split or adventurer card (CR
709.3, CR 715.3) - the same string `Action.spell_face` publishes and
`CastRequest.spell_face` takes back. CR 709.3b makes the chosen half's
own text the one the announcement is read against, so asking without it
answers the front half's targeting for both halves: Wear // Tear offered
Wear's "target artifact" while Tear was being cast.

Nothing here is hidden information: every candidate is an object in a
public zone (`affordances.CANDIDATE_ZONES`) or a player, so this needs no
`visibility.redact_view` pass of its own.

post.description:
File the post-game AI review (`mtg_agent.driver.review`, run on Opus
from a seat's own reflection plus the game's review record) -
`audit.AI_REVIEW_ACTION`, a row entirely separate from
`audit.REFLECTION_ACTION`.

Mirrors `declare_reflection` exactly: same gate (post-game only, against
`store.archived` so a soft-deleted lobby game still accepts one), same
uid-owns-seat check, same "mutates no `Game`" shape. See that route's
docstring for the reasoning; nothing here differs beyond which action
the row is filed under and whose words it carries.

**One check `declare_reflection` does not need: `req.player` must be a
registered AI seat of this game (`archived.ai_players`).** A reflection
is legitimately a human's own words about their own game; an AI review
is never that - it is only ever the output of an AI seat's own driver
critiquing that seat's play, so a human's own uid (which genuinely opens
their own seat, and would otherwise pass the check above) must not be
able to file one in anybody's name. Without this a human player could
forge a review of themselves or of their opponent, since the uid check
alone only proves "this credential speaks for this seat", not "this
seat is the kind that ever calls this route" - the same distinction
`AiReviewIn`'s docstring draws in words.

Record that the post-game AI review could NOT be produced, and why -
`audit.AI_REVIEW_FAILED_ACTION`.

Gated identically to `declare_ai_review` beside it, down to the AI-seat
check: only an AI seat's own driver ever generates a review, so only it
can report that one failed, and a human's own uid must not be able to
write "your review failed" into anybody's ledger.

**Why a route at all.** The driver is a separate process from this api
and reaches it only over HTTP, so a durable signal it can write has to be
a route. The alternative - leaving the four failures in the driver's own
`log.warning` calls - is what made "the reviewer failed" and "the
reviewer was never invoked" indistinguishable once a pod's logs rolled.
See `audit.AI_REVIEW_FAILED_ACTION` for why this row is not loud.
